assessments.strategy: Deliver deeper, sustained mTOR kinase inhibition in brain than rapalogs achieve, using an ATP-competitive (TORC1/2) inhibitor with CNS exposure. Practical sequencing: (1) benchmark CNS-penetrant tool compounds (TC1/related) head-to-head against everolimus in Tsc1-GFAP CKO and Tsc2 hypomorph seizure models with brain pS6/p4E-BP1/pAKT-S473 PD and free-brain-fraction PK; (2) in parallel, test whether any clinical-stage ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor can be repurposed at a paediatric-tolerable chronic dose — none was designed for CNS, so the honest expectation is that new chemistry (brain-penetrant, non-genotoxic, P-gp-sparing) is required; (3) consider preserving the rapalog tolerability profile by combining a low-dose rapalog with intermittent/pulsed catalytic dosing rather than chronic full TORC1/2 blockade.
existing_agents: Everolimus - approved (SEGA, renal AML, TSC-associated refractory seizures) - allosteric FKBP12-mTORC1 inhibitor; partial inhibition, limited brain penetration - PMID:24729041; PMID:30169322
Sirolimus - approved (LAM) / off-label TSC - allosteric mTORC1 inhibitor - ChEMBL/label
Vistusertib (AZD2014) - Phase 2 (oncology) - ATP-competitive mTORC1/2 inhibitor - ChEMBL CHEMBL2842
Sapanisertib (TAK-228/MLN0128) - Phase 2 (oncology) - ATP-competitive mTORC1/2 inhibitor - ChEMBL CHEMBL2842
AZD8055 - Phase 1 (halted, hepatotoxicity signal in oncology development) - ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor - ChEMBL CHEMBL2842
Dactolisib (BEZ235), omipalisib, gedatolisib, voxtalisib, apitolisib - Phase 1-3 (oncology) - dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitors; broader toxicity, not CNS-optimized - ChEMBL CHEMBL2842

TC1 and congeners - preclinical tool compounds only - brain-penetrant ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors; genotoxicity/exposure/primate tolerability liabilities reported - PMID:37399505; PMID:37545094
disease_relevant_cells: Dysmorphic neurons and giant cells in cortical tubers

delivery_feasibility.target_tissue: Brain — cortical tubers, perituberal cortex, subependymal zone
delivery_feasibility.target_cell: Dysmorphic neurons, giant cells, astrocytes; secondarily SEGA cells
delivery_feasibility.expected_access: Oral small molecule; SEGA and periventricular lesions sit at a leaky BBB/CSF interface and are already reached by everolimus (EVIDENCE, supportive, PMID:24729041). Diffuse cortex and perituberal tissue are the hard compartment: adequate free-brain concentration requires low P-gp efflux and high unbound fraction, which no clinical-stage ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor was optimized for (INFERENCE, contradictory).
delivery_feasibility.major_constraint: Not organ access but therapeutic window: mTOR is essential in all CNS and peripheral cells, so the limit is tolerated systemic exposure, not BBB crossing per se. Brain-selective PK (or intermittent dosing) is the only realistic way to widen it.

supporting_evidence.statement: Adjunctive everolimus significantly reduced treatment-refractory seizures versus placebo in TSC (EXIST-3), establishing that pharmacological mTOR inhibition is anti-seizure in humans and that more complete inhibition is a rational escalation.

Brain-penetrant ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors were developed specifically because everolimus penetrates brain poorly and inhibits mTOR only partially; leads normalized aberrant brain mTOR signalling and extended survival of neuronal Tsc1-knockout mice.

The brain-penetrant catalytic inhibitor TC1 reduced seizure burden in a Tsc2 hypomorphic model with a translationally relevant spontaneous seizure phenotype — i.e. the perturbation is executable in vivo with a small molecule.

A chemically mature class exists (vistusertib, sapanisertib, AZD8055 and others reached Phase 1-2), so medicinal chemistry for ATP-competitive mTOR inhibition is solved; the unmet requirement is CNS-optimization and chronic paediatric tolerability.
Higher seizure response in children (46%) than adults (14%) implies that in young patients residual disease may still be signalling-dependent and therefore addressable by deeper target engagement.

contradictory_evidence.statement: The published brain-penetrant catalytic inhibitors are explicitly tool compounds, not candidates: in vitro genotoxicity risk, poor oral exposure in higher species, and dose-limiting toxicity in cynomolgus macaque.

Oncology ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors have not produced a chronically dosable agent; AZD8055 and dual PI3K/mTOR compounds stalled at Phase 1-2, consistent with narrow windows for continuous TORC1/2 blockade.

mTORC2/AKT-S473 signalling is required for normal neuronal and metabolic function; abolishing the mTORC2 sparing that makes rapalogs chronically tolerable is a plausible mechanism-based toxicity in a developing child.
No TSC clinical trial of a catalytic mTOR inhibitor was identified in a ClinicalTrials.gov search of the condition; the TSC trial landscape is rapalogs, cannabidiol, ganaxolone and other ASMs.
Lesion regrowth after rapalog withdrawal implies cytostatic, suppressive action; deeper inhibition may deepen suppression without changing the need for lifelong therapy.

assessments.biggest_unknown: Whether residual seizures on everolimus reflect insufficient brain target engagement (measurable: does normalizing brain p4E-BP1 abolish seizures in a model where everolimus does not?) or fixed circuit pathology. Until a model experiment separates these, the whole programme rests on an untested premise.
assessments.biggest_failure_mode: Mechanism-based narrowing of the therapeutic window: the compound works in mice but chronic TORC1/2 inhibition at brain-effective exposure is intolerable in children (immunosuppression, growth, metabolic, neurodevelopmental mTORC2 loss), so the differentiating deep inhibition can never be dosed. Secondary failure mode: no de-risked chemical starting point exists — current brain-penetrant leads carry genotoxicity and primate tolerability liabilities, so this is a multi-year discovery programme, not repurposing.
assessments.conclusion_note: The perturbation is pharmacologically executable in rodents (PMID:37545094) but there is no clinical-stage, CNS-optimized, chronically dosable catalytic mTOR inhibitor. Honest framing for funders: this is novel chemistry with a mechanism-based window problem, and the cheap decisive experiment is a model study asking whether deeper brain mTOR inhibition actually outperforms optimally dosed everolimus on seizures.

assessments.strategy: Use EEG-triggered presymptomatic dosing in genetically diagnosed TSC infants. Agents are already approved: vigabatrin (GABA-transaminase inhibitor) for spasm/epilepsy prevention, and everolimus/sirolimus to act on the causal driver during the same window. Given PREVeNT, the defensible design is no longer 'vigabatrin prevents disability' but (a) vigabatrin at first epileptiform EEG for the epilepsy/spasm endpoint only, and (b) a separate test of early mTOR inhibition with neurodevelopmental endpoints, where the causal rationale is distinct from GABAergic seizure suppression.
existing_agents: Vigabatrin - approved (infantile spasms, refractory complex partial seizures) - irreversible GABA transaminase inhibitor; used presymptomatically in EPISTOP and PREVeNT - PMID:33180985; PMID:37638552

Everolimus - approved for TSC-associated seizures, SEGA, AML - allosteric mTORC1 inhibitor; paediatric PK and chronic safety already established, which is the key enabler for infant dosing - PMID:30169322
Sirolimus - approved (LAM), off-label paediatric TSC - allosteric mTORC1 inhibitor
Cannabidiol (GWP42003-P) - approved for TSC seizures after GWPCARE6 - non-mTOR adjunctive ASM; relevant comparator but not a prevention agent - NCT02544763
Ganaxolone - Phase 2 completed in TSC - neuroactive steroid GABA-A modulator - NCT04285346
disease_relevant_cells: Cortical neurons and interneurons in epileptogenic perituberal cortex
Dysmorphic neurons / giant cells in tubers
Neural progenitors during late prenatal/early postnatal circuit formation

delivery_feasibility.target_cell: Neurons/interneurons (vigabatrin, via GABA-T in neurons and astrocytes) and tuber cells/astrocytes/progenitors (mTOR inhibitors)
delivery_feasibility.expected_access: Vigabatrin is CNS-penetrant and orally dosed in infants as standard of care (EVIDENCE, supportive, PMID:37638552). Everolimus reaches SEGA and reduces seizures in children, so functionally relevant CNS engagement is proven, though diffuse cortical exposure is likely submaximal (EVIDENCE/INFERENCE, PMID:30169322).
delivery_feasibility.major_constraint: Not molecular delivery but the clinical window: identifying infants early enough requires genetic/prenatal diagnosis plus serial video-EEG surveillance infrastructure, and treating children who may never become symptomatic forces a hard risk-benefit (vigabatrin retinal toxicity; chronic everolimus immunosuppression in infancy).

supporting_evidence.statement: EPISTOP prospectively showed epileptiform discharges preceded clinical seizures in 54 of 94 seizure-naive TSC infants under monthly video-EEG, proving a detectable, actionable presymptomatic window.

Timing and features of the first epileptiform EEG predicted epilepsy and 24-month neurodevelopmental outcome, with earlier abnormality in TSC2 — giving a biomarker for both triggering and stratifying treatment.
Reviews of EPISTOP/PREVeNT conclude early vigabatrin may reduce refractory epilepsy and epileptic spasms, supporting presymptomatic EEG surveillance for seizure-focused endpoints.

Both candidate drug classes are already approved with paediatric dosing, so this hypothesis needs trial design and surveillance infrastructure, not new chemistry — by far the lowest pharmacological risk of the three hypotheses.
The much higher everolimus seizure response in children than adults is consistent with greater reversibility earlier in development, motivating testing mTOR inhibition inside the window.

contradictory_evidence.statement: PREVeNT, a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of vigabatrin at first epileptiform EEG versus at seizure onset, found no improvement in Bayley-III cognitive score at 24 months and did not decrease focal seizures. This directly falsifies the cognitive-prevention claim for presymptomatic vigabatrin.
PREVeNT 36-month follow-up reported cognitive scores declining slightly in all groups, with no signal that early vigabatrin prevented intellectual disability or ASD.

PREVeNT was also compromised as a prevention test because 19 of 27 placebo infants crossed to open-label vigabatrin at a median of 44 days, shrinking the exposure difference between arms — so it is a weaker falsification of 'very early treatment' than of 'vigabatrin at first EEG'.
EPISTOP could not randomize at 4 of 10 centres, producing an open-label arm and requiring bias-corrected re-analysis; the prevention evidence base is therefore weaker than trial labels suggest.
Vigabatrin causes irreversible retinal field loss, hard to justify in infants who may never become symptomatic, and PREVeNT removes the cognitive benefit that would have offset it.

No trial of presymptomatic mTOR inhibition in seizure-naive TSC infants was identified in the ClinicalTrials.gov condition search, so the arm with the strongest causal rationale is the one that has not been tested.

assessments.biggest_unknown: Whether any postnatal intervention can move cognition/ASD, i.e. how much TAND is prenatally fixed. PREVeNT is the first serious negative answer for a GABAergic drug; whether a causal-pathway drug (mTOR inhibitor) started at first epileptiform EEG does better is genuinely untested and is the decision-relevant question.
assessments.biggest_failure_mode: Repeating PREVeNT's outcome: the drug engages its target and may suppress EEG/spasms, yet the neurodevelopmental endpoint does not move because the injury is prenatal — compounded by rapid crossover to open-label rescue, which structurally prevents a prevention trial from ever showing a difference. Any next trial must pre-specify how it avoids the crossover problem and should power on seizure/EEG endpoints while treating cognition as secondary.
assessments.conclusion_note: Pharmacology is fully in hand (approved agents, infant dosing established); the binding constraint is trial design and a now-negative randomized result for the vigabatrin-cognition version. Recommended reframing: fund presymptomatic mTOR inhibition with EEG-triggered entry, not another vigabatrin cognition trial.

assessments.strategy: Test whether small-molecule blockade of VEGFR, TGF-beta/ALK5 or the IL-1/caspase-1 axis reduces seizures on top of (not instead of) optimally dosed rapamycin in Tsc1-GFAP CKO or Tsc2 hypomorph mice. The add-on design is the whole point: it is the only way to distinguish an mTOR-independent driver from a reversible downstream readout. Only if add-on benefit is seen does an agent-selection problem arise — and at that point the CNS-penetrant options are thin.
existing_agents: Apatinib - approved (China, gastric cancer) - VEGFR2 tyrosine kinase inhibitor; used as the VEGFR intervention in the Tsc1-GFAP CKO study - PMID:38049961
RepSox - preclinical tool compound only - TGF-beta receptor I (ALK5) inhibitor, used as BBB stabilizer in the same study - PMID:38049961

Other approved VEGFR TKIs (sunitinib, axitinib, pazopanib, cediranib) - approved (oncology) - VEGFR1-3 inhibition; chronic paediatric use constrained by hypertension, growth-plate and vascular toxicity - INFERENCE

VX-765 / belnacasan - Phase 2 (epilepsy, discontinued) - caspase-1 inhibitor, reduces IL-1beta maturation; the only CNS-oriented small-molecule IL-1 axis agent - INFERENCE, not retrieved in this search
Anakinra / canakinumab - approved - IL-1 blockade, but these are proteins, not small molecules, and brain penetration is poor; defer to the protein agent
disease_relevant_cells: Astrocytes (source of IL-1beta and CXCL10 in Tsc1-GFAP CKO)
Brain microvascular endothelial cells and pericytes (BBB integrity)
Cortical neurons as the downstream victim cell

delivery_feasibility.target_tissue: Brain microvasculature and perituberal cortical parenchyma
delivery_feasibility.expected_access: Endothelial targets are the most accessible in principle, since a luminal VEGFR2 on brain endothelium is reachable from blood without crossing the BBB (INFERENCE, supportive). Astrocytic/microglial IL-1 signalling requires true parenchymal penetration; VEGFR TKIs such as apatinib are P-gp substrates with limited CNS exposure, and anti-IL-1 biologics do not cross (INFERENCE, contradictory). RepSox is a tool compound with no clinical development path.
delivery_feasibility.major_constraint: Cell-type mismatch: the readily drugged compartment (endothelium) is not clearly the seizure-driving compartment (astrocyte/neuron), and the agents that hit the astrocytic target are either non-CNS-penetrant or non-clinical. Add to this the unacceptability of chronic anti-VEGF/anti-angiogenic therapy in growing children.

supporting_evidence.statement: Tsc1-GFAP CKO mice show elevated brain VEGF, abnormal cerebral vessel anatomy and two-photon-confirmed BBB leak, and a VEGFR antagonist (apatinib) plus a BBB stabilizer (RepSox) were applied as interventions — establishing both a druggable node and a model readout.
IL-1beta and CXCL10 are increased in neocortex and hippocampus of Tsc1-GFAP CKO mice, localized mainly to astrocytes, and anti-inflammatory treatment was tested against epilepsy in this model.

Approved VEGFR TKIs and IL-1 pathway agents exist, so a proof-of-concept add-on experiment in mice can be run quickly and cheaply with off-the-shelf compounds — the hypothesis is testable now even if it is not yet a clinical plan.

contradictory_evidence.statement: The inflammatory markers in this model were themselves reversed by mTORC1 inhibition, which is the signature of a downstream consequence rather than an mTOR-independent driver; blocking them may add nothing on top of a rapalog.
No human TSC trial of VEGF or IL-1 pathway blockade for epilepsy was identified in the ClinicalTrials.gov condition search; the clinical TSC pipeline contains no agent of this class.

Chronic VEGFR inhibition in children causes hypertension, impaired wound healing and growth-plate effects, and anti-angiogenic therapy in a developing brain is a poor fit for a lifelong non-malignant indication.
Evidence rests on a single conditional-knockout model and the magnitude of seizure benefit relative to mTOR inhibition was not quantified in what was retrieved.
The two agents actually used in the supporting study are a China-only oncology TKI and a non-clinical tool compound, so even a positive mouse result would not hand you a translatable molecule.

assessments.biggest_unknown: Whether these changes contribute causally and mTOR-independently to seizures. This is decidable in one well-powered add-on experiment (rapamycin alone versus rapamycin + apatinib/IL-1 blockade versus vehicle, with seizure burden by continuous EEG), and that experiment should gate any further investment.
assessments.biggest_failure_mode: Epiphenomenon: the axis is a faithful biomarker of mTORC1 hyperactivation with no independent causal contribution, so add-on therapy gives zero incremental seizure benefit and the programme dies after the mouse study. The second, equally likely failure is agent-level: even a true effect cannot be exploited because the CNS-penetrant, chronically-dosable-in-children molecule for the astrocytic IL-1 node does not exist.
assessments.conclusion_note: Mechanistically interesting and cheap to falsify, but currently one-model evidence, an explicitly mTOR-reversible readout, no clinical agent in TSC, and a cell-type/penetration mismatch. Fund the add-on mouse experiment as a small gated study; do not plan a clinical path yet.
